newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Parliament ratifies South Korea's entry to OECD.
newsitem.headline: Parliament ratifies South Korea's entry to OECD.

text.p: South Korea on Tuesday removed the last hurdle to joining the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) when parliament voted to ratify the country's membership in the club of established economies.
Seoul officials said President Kim Young-sam would soon sign the membership agreement, expanding the OECD to 29 countries and giving the Paris-based club greater weight in Asia.
South Korea will be the second Asian member after Japan and the first from the region's newly industrialised economies.
A total of 159 members of the 299-seat National Assembly voted in favour of OECD membership while 101 opposed the move, officials said. Two of the 262 members present abstained.

Seoul was invited to join the OECD on October 11, but members of the opposition had threatened to block ratification in parliament, saying the OECD could force Korea to open its local markets to foreign competition too quickly.
Park Kwang-tae, a lawmaker with the main opposition National Congress for New Politics, told parliament his party was not opposed to OECD membership in principle, but wanted to wait.
"The troubled economy cannot withstand the shock of excessive market liberalisation," Park said.
Since applying for OECD membership in March 1995, South Korea has accelerated the opening of its financial markets to foreign investors and pledged further reforms.
Last month, it raised the limit on the amount of shares in listed Korean firms that can be held by foreigners to 20 percent from 18 percent. The ceiling is due to rise to 23 percent next year.
But critics have said the rapid opening of the financial markets could deal a blow to the economy, already suffering from a growing trade deficit and inflationary pressures.
The government projects the nation's current-account deficit will rise to about $20 billion in calendar 1996 from a shortfall of $8.9 billion in 1995.

Chang Che-shik, also from the National Congress of New Politics, accused the government of trying to "create the fantasy that our country is an advanced country" to help Kim's party's chances in next year's presidential election.

"It would not be too late for the country to join the OECD after first examining the pros and cons carefully and preparing for the destabilising effects of speeding up opening of markets, particularly in small- and medium-sized industries," he said.

Opposition members said they feared entry into the OECD would hamper the economy by triggering an influx of speculative funds into local markets as foreign investors try to benefit from South Korea's relatively high interest rates. Interest on a one-year time deposit is around 12 percent.
But Hyun Jung-taik, director-general of the Finance Ministry's international economic policy bureau, said Seoul would ensure stability by adhering to a timetable for opening markets.
Government officials said that even if the economy was slowing down after a sustained period of strong growth, it was time that South Korea was accepted in the OECD.
South Korea's central bank expects gross domestic product to grow by nearly seven percent in real terms this year against last year's nine percent.

Cha Soo-myong, a legislator with the ruling New Korea Party, said entry into the OECD would allow South Korea to increase links with advanced economies and thereby hasten its own economic development. "Liberalisation of the economy will eventually make our country more competitive," he said.
